title: KiaKio and Squared Numbers
solution: The map f(x) = sum of squared decimal digits is a functional graph: any x <= 10^9 drops to <= 729 after one step, and every trajectory then falls within about a dozen steps into either the fixed point 1 or the 8-cycle 4->16->37->58->89->145->42->20->4. Two lighthouses are in tune iff their trajectories coincide from some night on, which (since f is deterministic) holds iff f^T(a_i) = f^T(a_j) for one sufficiently large common T (past every tail). So simulate every a_i for a fixed T (e.g. 100) steps, then group the final values in a hash map and add C(cnt, 2) for each group. Values in the 8-cycle only match when they are at the same phase, which comparing at a common T captures automatically. Complexity O(n * T * digits), trivial for sum n <= 1000.

solution_check.how: Python script with T=100 reproduces all four sample answers (1, 6, 0, 1); also checked that the maximum tail length into {1} or the 8-cycle over all starts <= 999 is 11.

rejected_patterns.reason: No cycle is ever detected: no visited set, no Floyd/Brent, no repeat check. Because f is deterministic (once two lighthouses agree they agree forever), comparing f^T(a_i) with f^T(a_j) at one common large T is the definition read directly. T=100 (anything >= 12 works; max tail into {1} or the 8-cycle is 11 after the first step) reproduces all samples and matched an O(n^2) trajectory brute force on 300 random tests. Unlike Badge (CF 1020B), where you walk until a vertex repeats, nothing here needs a repeat found.

The successor structure of x -> digit-square-sum is statement structure, not a technique the solution uses. Nobody builds the graph or computes tails, cycle ids or phases; the phase subtlety (16 and 2 are both on the cycle but never match) goes away when every value is advanced the same number of steps. The only reasoning needed is that values drop to <= 729 after one step, so orbits become periodic within a bounded number of steps (pigeonhole), which is simulation-bound reasoning. Someone searching functional-graph (Planets Queries, Robots on a Grid) would get a 5-line fixed-step simulation.
Scaffolding: with sum n <= 1000, even an O(n^2) pairwise comparison of final values works; the C(cnt,2) grouping by value is bookkeeping, not a counting technique.

rejected_tags.reason: Pair counting here is bookkeeping (O(n^2) comparison suffices for sum n <= 1000), not a combinatorial counting idea.

notes.solver: The core insight is functional-graph structure (tails into the fixed point 1 or the 8-cycle, where phase matters); simulating a fixed large number of steps and comparing values avoids any explicit cycle-finding, so cycle-detection gets lower confidence (it is included because the problem is about eventual periodicity and cycle phase). Counting equal-value pairs via a hash map is minor. Rejected: number-theory (digit-square sums are not really number theory here), brute-force (subsumed by simulation).
notes.skeptic: Answer to the brief: fixed-step simulation is all anyone writes; neither cycle-detection nor functional-graph is used. Solution verified: simulating every a_i for T=100 steps and grouping final values gives 1,6,0,1 on the samples and matched a direct brute force (checks whether the trajectories are equal from some night k on) on 300 random tests. The only cycles among 1..999 are {1} and 4->16->37->58->89->145->42->20; max tail length is 11. The summary was rewritten to name the technique-deciding fact (one step brings values to <= 729, so they settle quickly and fixed-step simulation works) instead of implying phase tracking is needed. It keeps the words '8-cycle' and 'cycle phase' so lexical search still finds it. The proposal's max value (729) is correct. Only one pattern is left, which suits a Div2-B simulation.
